newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Friction marks Britain-China wrangle on HK future.
newsitem.headline: Friction marks Britain-China wrangle on HK future.

text.p: Just 34 days before Hong Kong changes rulers, friction emerged on Wednesday when Britain and China launched into a final round of diplomatic haggling on the historic handover.
A meeting of the Joint Liaison Group (JLG), headed by ambassadors from the two countries, immediately produced divergent views over the future of their own forum.

Britain wants it to monitor compliance with the 1984 Sino-British handover treaty and other documents that promised Hong Kong a high degree of autonomy and the preservation of its capitalist way of life. China sees a much lower-key role.

China's chief negotiator Zhao Jihua told reporters the JLG will just be a liaison body following the handover, and suggested that Britain should focus less on the post-change period and more on unresolved handover problems.
But British team leader Hugh Davies said it would continue to discuss the handover treaty known as the Joint Declaration well beyond the change of flag at midnight June 30.
"There will certainly be ongoing discussions about the joint declaration right through the period of the JLG's existence," Davies told reporters.
Under the treaty, the JLG is supposed to continue to meet at least three times annually until the year 2000.
An official said the three-day session would also try to "cross the t's, dot the i's on the joint handover ceremony".

A midnight extravaganza, to be attended by 4,000 VIPs including Chinese and British leaders, will bid farewell to 156 years of colonial rule with a military pageant, a solemn flag raising ceremony and a sky full of fireworks.

A big political quarrel is raging between pro-China and pro-democracy forces in Hong Kong over future leader Tung Chee-hwa's plan, inspired by China, to reverse the liberal electoral reforms of departing Governor Chris Patten.
Patten and other critics say it is designed to hamper the popular Democratic Party from winning seats in 1998 elections.

After an avalanche of criticism for not consulting the public, Tung did a U-turn on Tuesday and agreed to accept comments from the community over the next two weeks before finalising the new election rules.
The JLG will also tackle "legal issues" and the transfer of Hong Kong government assets and archives to the new government.
It will be the 40th round of JLG talks since they began in 1985 as a bargaining shop to elaborate on details of the handover, based on the 1984 pact.
Over the years the talks have produced accords on areas such as the construction of a new airport, due to open next April.

It also produced a deal allowing China to send advance troops of the People's Liberation Army garrison into Hong Kong before the handover, another on the sell-off of former defence lands, and a government budget to straddle the handover.
But ideological disputes over human rights and democracy have dogged the JLG, with China's bloody 1989 crackdown on pro-democracy protests in Beijing hardening Britain's stance.
One analyst said the JLG had basically "prepared the ground to turn Hong Kong from a British colony into a Chinese colony".

The handover ceremony deal remained elusive until recently. And no agreement has been reached on vital issues such as the right of abode of Hong Kong people, or China's plans to dilute democracy and reshape Hong Kong's political system.

Rejecting fierce critcism from Britain and from Hong Kong democrats, China will dissolve the elected legislature and install a provisional lawmaking body on July 1, and liberal civil rights and electoral laws will be stiffened.
